screens.heading: Three branches
screens.body: The officer will ask how American government is built — questions like:
screens.afterQuote: This lesson will help you answer those questions.
screens.coverageLine: It covers 20 of the 128 on the test.
screens.afterTest: And after the test: this is how to understand any news story about Washington.

screens.question: Imagine one person writes the rules, enforces the rules, AND judges everyone accused of breaking them. Good idea or bad idea?
screens.feedback: The founders' answer: very bad idea. They had just escaped a ruler with too much power. So they split the power into three.

bodyList: In a soccer game, the players do not referee themselves, and the referee does not write the rulebook — three different hands, on purpose.
At work, the person who spends the money is usually not the person who checks the books.
bodyList2: When one person holds every job, honest mistakes go uncorrected and dishonest ones go unpunished.
Splitting the jobs is how groups protect themselves.
screens.closing: America built its whole government on that idea.

cards.example: A branch of government is like one branch of a tree.

cards.def: to say no to a bill.
cards.example: The President can veto a bill — say no to it.

cards.def: to make people follow a rule.
a judge on the Supreme Court.
cards.example: There are nine justices on the Supreme Court.

paragraphs: The Capitol: Congress works here — it writes the laws. Congress has two parts, the Senate and the House of Representatives; you will meet them closely in the next lesson.

The White House: the President works here — the President carries out the laws, leads the executive branch, commands the military as Commander in Chief, and leads a team: the Vice President, the Cabinet, and the federal departments and agencies.
The Supreme Court: nine justices work here — the courts explain the laws, resolve disputes about them, and decide whether a law goes against the Constitution.
screens.handle: Congress makes the laws. The President carries them out. The courts explain them.
screens.handleSub: No branch can do another branch's job.
screens.alt: Three government buildings side by side: the domed Capitol, the White House, and the columned Supreme Court.

paragraphs: Now watch the buildings push against each other.
Congress passes a bill. It is not law yet — it goes to the President, who signs it into law or vetoes it. And even a signed law can be stopped: a court can rule it goes against the Constitution.

Each branch can block the others. That blocking has a name you already know from the rulebook lesson: checks and balances — also called separation of powers. It exists for one reason: so no one part becomes too powerful. The same reason answers three different test questions.

One more piece of the same idea: Supreme Court justices serve for life. Why? If a judge could be fired, that judge would be afraid of the people above them. A judge who serves for life has no one to fear — so they are free to follow only the rulebook, not politics. That independence is the whole point.
screens.resolution: It usually takes five of the nine justices to decide a case. The President appoints federal judges — but cannot remove them.
screens.handle: Checks and balances exist so no one part becomes too powerful.

screens.heading: Each branch can stop the others. That is the design working.
screens.example: Congress writes a bill raising a tax. The President vetoes it. The bill does not become law — unless a very large majority in Congress votes again to overrule the veto. Two branches, pushing.
screens.nonExample: A king announces a tax in the morning, collects it that same afternoon, and puts anyone who complains in prison that night. One person, all three jobs — the exact thing the three buildings exist to prevent.
screens.takeaway: Splitting the jobs is what stops any one of them from becoming a king.

screens.heading: Two names on the test sound alike. Do not mix them up.

termA.name: The Cabinet
termA.def: advises the President. It is a small team of people the President chooses.

termB.name: Congress
termB.def: writes the laws. It has 535 members, and they are elected by voters — not chosen by the President.

screens.resolution: The President picks the Cabinet. Voters pick Congress.

items.question: A bill is written. Before it becomes law, whose desk must it cross — and what two things can happen there?
options: The President's — who signs it into law, or vetoes it
The Chief Justice's — who approves it, or strikes it down
The Speaker's — who publishes it, or delays it

items.question: Why can a court stop a law that Congress and the President both approved?
options: Because the Constitution is above all three of them
Because judges are elected by the people
Because the President asked them to

items.question: The officer asks this. Is the first word asking for a list, or a reason?
items.cardText: There are three branches of government. Why?
options: A reason — because no one part should become too powerful
A list — legislative, executive, and judicial
items.pairedOfficial: There are three branches of government. Why?

screens.feedbackExplain: A justice serves for life so that no one can remove them for a decision. A judge with no one to fear is free to follow only the rulebook.
